units.title: Instruction pipelines, branches and SIMD
outcomes: Explain pipeline overlap, instruction dependencies and branch recovery without equating clock cycles with instructions.
Identify SIMD lanes, loop tails and a loop-carried dependency in compiler output.
Separate a compiler's vectorization decision from evidence of a runtime speedup.
units.why: Assume Programming's layout-alignment-locality and profiling-benchmarking units. Here the mechanism is instruction execution: dependencies, speculation and SIMD determine which work can overlap before the kernel or storage enters the picture.

next.note: Explain why wider arithmetic still has to wait for data.

study.title: Pipelining & Performance
study.locator: Iron Law of Processor Performance; Pipelined Processors; Performance of Pipelined Processors; Latency vs. Throughput; Hazards
study.depth: Use the ideal five-stage calculation and the control-hazard example. Do not transfer its CPI or stage count to the i9, or follow the textbook pointer into full processor design.

study.title: Loop vectorization and its limits
study.locator: Usage; Diagnostics; Features: Loops with unknown trip count, Runtime Checks of Pointers, Reductions, If Conversion and Partial unrolling during vectorization
study.depth: Stop before Epilogue Vectorization. Skip historical Performance charts; they are not measurements of this machine.

focus: Pipeline overlap improves throughput, not necessarily the latency of one instruction. Dependencies limit overlap; a wrong branch prediction discards speculative work.
Instruction count, CPI and clock period all enter execution time. Out-of-order execution schedules ready work but must preserve architectural behavior.
SIMD widens independent operations. Tails, alias checks, calls and recurrences constrain the generated loop; unrolling is not itself SIMD.
If conversion can replace branches. Inspect the executable before calling an input-order timing difference a branch-prediction effect.
units.reproduce: From a blank C file, write noinline bump(uint32_t *a, unsigned n) with a[i] += 1u for i=0..n-1, and noinline chain with a[i] += a[i-1] for i=1..n-1. In main initialize 1031 elements to i, call bump, sum into uint64_t and print it, then call chain and print a[1030]. Compile with clang -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -Rpass=loop-vectorize -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize, and again with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize. Run both with taskset -c 2. Both print 531996 twice. On Clang 21.1.8, bump vectorizes with eight uint32_t lanes and chain does not; confirm packed additions and the scalar tail with objdump -d. This is a correctness and instruction observation, not a timing claim.
traps: Counting SIMD lanes as a promised speedup. Loads, stores, dependencies and loop overhead still consume resources.
Using signed overflow or floating-point reassociation as an exact correctness oracle. Use unsigned arithmetic here; floating-point reductions need a stated error criterion.
Timing a loop the compiler folded away, or attributing branch misses to source-level if statements that became branchless code.

selfTest.q: In an ideal five-stage pipeline with no stalls, how many cycles complete ten instructions?
selfTest.a: Four fill cycles plus ten completions: 14 cycles. This is a model, not a measurement of the host CPU.

selfTest.q: Why does chain not have the same independent lanes as bump?
selfTest.a: Iteration i needs the value written by iteration i-1. A simple widening would read the wrong predecessor; a different algorithm such as a parallel scan is needed.

selfTest.q: Does a vectorization remark prove the vector loop ran for a particular call?
selfTest.a: No. A small length, tail or runtime alias check can select a scalar path. Inspect the call's inputs and generated control flow.

selfTest.q: Can a predictable branch be cheaper than computing both arms?
selfTest.a: Yes. Prediction can avoid unnecessary work. Which version wins depends on the generated code and workload and must be measured.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a correctness-checked scalar/vectorized kernel, dependency and branch variants, saved assembly, and pinned repeated measurements with compiler flags and warm-up state.
units.stopWhen: Both builds agree on the checksum and recurrence endpoint, and you can mark the vector lanes, scalar tail and dependency in the executable without promising a speedup.

fit.note: The selected OS pool does not locate pipelines or SIMD at working depth. Cornell supplies the pipeline model and LLVM supplies current, executable vectorization guidance; the mini-project supplies performance practice.

units.title: Caches, working sets, bandwidth and NUMA
outcomes: Explain cache-line fills, coherence and false sharing separately from language-level synchronization.
Measure a traversal-order change with a fixed working set and a correctness oracle.
Estimate useful bytes and line traffic with units, and distinguish bandwidth from dependent-load latency.
Explain CPU affinity and NUMA page placement without claiming remote-memory measurements on a one-node host.
units.why: Assume Programming's layout-alignment-locality unit, including its AoS/SoA experiment. This unit moves to cache ownership, working-set regimes and physical placement rather than repeating that layout comparison.

next.note: Add translation and residency to the memory-access path.
Measure cache-line ownership traffic under actual multicore contention.

study.title: The Memory Hierarchy and Why Latency Matters
study.locator: CPU Caches through Memory Capacity vs. Memory Speed; A Simple Locality Experiment
study.depth: Correct the experiment before running it: its unmodified static matrix is all zero and GCC can remove the loops. Initialize every element to (row+column)&255 and declare the matrix volatile so both access orders remain. This measures scalar volatile traversal, not optimized application bandwidth.

study.title: Coherence and false sharing
study.locator: Cache Coherence vs. Memory Consistency; False Sharing: Independent Data, Shared Cache Line; True Sharing and False Sharing; Separating Frequently Written Data
study.depth: Leave atomics and the multicore benchmark to the concurrency section. A single-core-pinned run cannot demonstrate lines bouncing between cores.

study.title: NUMA placement vocabulary
study.locator: NUMA: Memory Locality through NUMA Problems in Backend Services
study.depth: Inspect topology only. This host has one NUMA node, so skip commands requiring node 1 and do not report a local/remote timing ratio.

focus: Read cpu2/cache/index*/{level,type,size,coherency_line_size,shared_cpu_list} under /sys/devices/system/cpu and run lscpu before estimating line traffic. Aggregate lscpu cache sizes are not per-core capacities.
A stream can overlap independent misses and use bandwidth; a pointer chain waits for each next address and exposes latency. Useful bytes/time is not automatically DRAM traffic/time.
Coherence coordinates writes to locations. It does not establish the language's cross-location publication order; false sharing is independent writers sharing one line.
Working-set fit, conflicts, prefetch, translation and frequency all affect a curve. CPU pinning does not relocate pages; NUMA distance values are not measured nanoseconds.
units.reproduce: Rebuild the corrected A Simple Locality Experiment from memory: a static volatile int matrix[4096][4096], initialized to (r+c)&255 before timing, with row-first and column-first sums into long long and CLOCK_MONOTONIC around each traversal. Build with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra and run taskset -c 2 ./locality five times. Each traversal sums to 2139095040; the array is 64 MiB when sizeof(int)==4. Record all timings, kernel, CPU and GCC version, and note that initialization touched all pages but a 64 MiB array cannot be wholly warm in this host's 30 MiB LLC. Do not assume either traversal wins. Derive line utilization using the inspected line size, then explain why TLB behavior and volatile loads prevent this from being a pure DRAM-bandwidth benchmark.
traps: Turning a slower strided run into a cache-miss count. Timing alone cannot separate cache, TLB, prefetch and instruction effects.
Using perf c2c or system-wide counters despite host permissions. Keep optional counters to your own pinned process and user-space cycles/instructions; cpu_core and cpu_atom are separate PMUs.
Reporting NUMA remote latency from this machine. There is no second memory node to measure.

selfTest.q: For an aligned array of four-byte integers and an inspected 64-byte line, how much of each line does a stride-16 pass use?
selfTest.a: One integer, or 4/64 = 1/16 of the line, before any later reuse. This is useful-byte utilization, not a measured memory-traffic multiplier.

selfTest.q: Why can two race-free counters still contend in hardware?
selfTest.a: Separate counters can share one cache line. Writes on different cores repeatedly require ownership of that line even though neither counter has multiple writers.

selfTest.q: Does a working set smaller than cache capacity guarantee hits?
selfTest.a: No. Conflicts, competing code/data and other users of shared cache can evict lines; compulsory fills still occur.

selfTest.q: What can numactl --hardware establish on a one-node host?
selfTest.a: Visible CPUs, node membership and node capacity. It cannot supply an observed remote-memory penalty.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: working-set and stride sweeps across inspected cache capacities, a dependent pointer chase versus a stream, matched checksums, pinned five-repeat raw timings, and a topology note explicitly excluding remote NUMA claims.
units.stopWhen: Both traversal checksums agree, your evidence records topology and cache state, and you can explain useful-byte traffic, latency versus bandwidth and a hypothetical false-sharing layout without treating timing as causal proof.

fit.note: The selected pool lacks located cache/coherence/NUMA teaching. Three owned AlgoMaster hardware lessons fill that coverage gap; corrected traversal and the mini-project give measured practice.

units.title: Processes, system calls, fork, exec and scheduling
outcomes: Trace fork, exec and wait while identifying kernel-owned state and preserved process identity.
Distinguish a privilege-mode transition from a scheduler context switch.
Implement child launch and status collection with an explicit exec-failure path.
Predict ready, running and blocked transitions under a stated scheduling model.
units.why: Assume Programming's shell-processes-environment unit and its exit-status and trap exercises. Here you trace the kernel process model, not shell syntax, and make the launcher own every child it creates.

next.note: Give the child deliberate I/O and termination ownership.

study.title: The process and its API
study.locator: Chapter 4, Sections 4.1 to 4.5 (Processes, linked from the book contents); Chapter 5, Sections 5.1 to 5.4, including Figures 5.1 to 5.4
study.depth: Read the redirection example for the fork/exec boundary; leave descriptor details to the next unit.

study.title: Protected execution and scheduling
study.locator: Chapter 6, Sections 6.1 to 6.3; Chapter 7, Sections 7.1 to 7.2 and 7.6 to 7.8 (CPU Scheduling, linked from the book contents)
study.depth: Treat round robin as a model, not Linux's normal scheduler. A context switch can disturb cache/TLB locality; it does not necessarily flush every cache or every tagged TLB entry.

study.title: Linux process launch and switching
study.locator: What exec Replaces and What It Preserves; Encoded Wait Status; Handling an Interrupted Wait; Multithreaded fork Considerations; Failure Handling by Operation
study.depth: Then use Context Switching, Mode Switches vs. Context Switches and Blocking, Preemption, and the State Model. Do not benchmark switch cost yet.

study.title: Xv6 utilities: the exec task
study.locator: exec: adding -exec cmd to find; hints on fork, exec and wait
study.depth: Read and sketch the lifecycle only. RISC-V tools and QEMU are not installed here, so do not claim a make grade result. Leave full util-lab completion to a provisioned course environment.

focus: Fork creates a child with a different PID; successful exec replaces its address space while retaining its PID. Wait consumes an owned child's termination record.
System calls enter controlled kernel code. A call can return in the same task without any switch to another task; blocking or preemption can cause scheduling.
Ready is not running, and blocked is not merely low CPU usage. Linux's R status includes running and runnable tasks.
Response time and turnaround time answer different questions. A policy comparison needs arrivals, CPU bursts, I/O durations and switch assumptions.
units.reproduce: Write a single-threaded Python launcher using os.fork, os.execl and os.waitpid. In the child, os.write its PID before exec; execute /bin/sh with arguments -c 'echo

; exit 7'. The parent waits for that PID and decodes WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS. Repeat with /atlas-missing-executable, catching OSError in the child and calling os._exit(127). Run taskset -c 2 strace -f -e trace=process -- /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I launcher.py. Match the pre/post-exec PID; verify normal exit 7 and launch failure 127. These are program-selected codes, not a universal exec-error encoding. Keep the trace showing process creation, execve and wait4; Linux's fork wrapper may use clone.
traps: Expecting the parent to run first after fork, or treating a sleep as a synchronization guarantee.
Returning through normal Python cleanup after a failed child exec. Use os._exit for this post-fork failure path and collect the result in the parent.
Extending this single-threaded fork pattern to a multithreaded runtime. Copied locks can remain owned by threads that no longer exist in the child.

selfTest.q: Does successful exec return zero to the old program?
selfTest.a: No. It does not return. Only failure returns to the old image; the kernel keeps the process identity but installs a new program image.

selfTest.q: What must happen after a blocked child's I/O completes before it executes again?
selfTest.a: It becomes runnable and the scheduler must select it. Completion does not imply immediate execution.

selfTest.q: Is every system call a context switch?
selfTest.a: No. It changes privilege mode, but another task need not run. A blocked call can lead to a context switch.

selfTest.q: Can the raw wait status be compared directly with exit code 7?
selfTest.a: No. First test normal exit with WIFEXITED and then decode WEXITSTATUS. Signaled termination has a different interpretation.

practice.name: OSTEP process-run.py: CPU/I/O state prediction
practice.locator: README Overview and process-run.py; use -s 1 and -s 2 with -l 5:50,5:100 -L 5
practice.note: Predict the full trace before adding -c -p. Compare SWITCH_ON_IO with SWITCH_ON_END and IO_RUN_LATER with IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE. The answer flag is the simulator's oracle, not a Linux scheduler test. Save one matching local launcher trace for the section evidence pack.

units.stopWhen: Your launcher reaps both success and exec-failure children, and your two-seed simulator predictions distinguish blocked time from ready time and a mode switch from a task switch.

fit.note: OSTEP provides process mechanisms and scheduling assumptions, AlgoMaster provides launch edge cases, and the named simulator plus a local traced launcher meet implement depth without an unavailable xv6 toolchain.

units.title: File descriptors, pipes, signals and process lifecycle
outcomes: Implement a parent-child pipe with deliberate redirection, closure and reaping on each path.
Predict shared open-file offsets and close-on-exec behavior across dup, fork and exec.
Diagnose a retained pipe writer or zombie from kernel state rather than from a timeout alone.
Distinguish signal notification, delivery, termination and status collection.
units.why: Assume Programming's shell-processes-environment unit, including signal exit conventions. This unit exposes descriptor references, pipe endpoint counts and child status records that make shell pipelines and process supervisors work.

next.note: Carry lifecycle ownership into a PID namespace.
Extend descriptor ownership and partial-I/O handling to byte-stream sockets.

study.title: Descriptor entries versus open descriptions
study.locator: The Three-Level Model through Descriptor Flags vs. File Status Flags; Observing Descriptors Through /proc; Demonstrating Shared and Independent Offsets

study.title: Signals and child ownership
study.locator: The Signal Lifecycle; Dispositions: Default, Ignore, or Catch; Why Handlers Must Be Tiny; Interrupted System Calls and EINTR; Signal Masks and Pending Signals; SIGCHLD: Notification, Not Reaping
study.depth: Then read Zombies and Orphans: What Exactly Is a Zombie?, Reaping Without Blocking, What Is an Orphan? and Subreapers and Process Supervisors. Leave multithreaded signal coordination to concurrency.

study.title: Wait status and child states
study.locator: DESCRIPTION: wait() and waitpid(), status macros, waitid() and WNOWAIT; NOTES on zombies

study.title: Offsets shared through fork and dup
study.locator: Chapter 39, Sections 39.4 to 39.6, especially Shared File Table Entries: fork() And dup()

focus: A descriptor entry holds its own close-on-exec flag; the open file description holds the shared offset and status flags. A repeated open creates independent open state.
After dup2, close unused pipe endpoints in both processes. EOF requires an empty pipe and no remaining write references; parent exit is not the definition of EOF.
Signals have dispositions and per-thread masks. SIGCHLD can coalesce; drain waitable children rather than counting notifications.
A zombie has already released its user memory and descriptors. An orphan changes parent; Linux can adopt it through a subreaper rather than the host PID 1.
units.reproduce:
Write a Python parent with two os.pipe pairs. Fork one child, dup2 its request-read end onto fd 0 and response-write end onto fd 1, close all original endpoints and execl /bin/cat. In the parent close the child-only ends, write b'abc
' with a partial-write loop, close the request writer, read the response until EOF and waitpid the child. Assert exactly b'abc
' and normal exit 0. Run strace -f -e trace=process,pipe,pipe2,dup2,read,write,close -- /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I pipes.py. In a separate empty pipe, set the reader nonblocking: retaining the writer gives BlockingIOError, closing the last writer gives b''. Finally fork a child that sets SIGTERM to SIG_DFL, announces readiness through a pipe and waits; signal it only after readiness. Use waitid with WEXITED|WNOWAIT to observe /proc/<pid>/status state Z, then waitpid and verify WIFSIGNALED with WTERMSIG==SIGTERM. Use no sleep as an ordering guarantee.
traps: Keeping a spare write descriptor open and waiting for EOF forever. Inheritance and duplication both retain references.
Assuming Python's newly created descriptors survive exec. They are non-inheritable by default; deliberate dup2 onto standard I/O is inheritable unless requested otherwise.
Calling arbitrary logging or allocation from a native signal handler, or assuming shell status 128+signal is the raw wait status.

selfTest.q: A child reads through an inherited regular-file descriptor. Does the parent's offset advance?
selfTest.a: Yes, if both entries still refer to the same inherited open file description. Separate open calls would have independent offsets.

selfTest.q: The producer exited, but an unrelated child inherited its pipe writer. Will an empty pipe return EOF?
selfTest.a: No. A write reference still exists. A blocking reader waits and a nonblocking reader reports EAGAIN until the last writer closes.

selfTest.q: Why does one SIGCHLD handler invocation not imply one terminated child?
selfTest.a: Standard signals can coalesce and SIGCHLD can report other child state changes. Reap in a loop with waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG), handling the documented return cases.

selfTest.q: Can SIGKILL remove a zombie's retained status record?
selfTest.a: No. It is already terminated. Its parent or adopter must collect the record; signal delivery is not reaping.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a supervised pipe worker with a descriptor ownership diagram, deliberate leaked-writer regression test, signal termination, zombie observation, and guaranteed closure and reaping on success and failure.
units.stopWhen: The pipe round trip passes, your nonblocking leak test distinguishes EAGAIN from EOF, and your signal test observes then reaps the zombie with a correctly decoded wait status.

fit.note: OSTEP and the selected AlgoMaster descriptor, signal and zombie lessons explain owned kernel state; wait(2) supplies the precise observation contract and the mini-project supplies implementation practice.

units.title: Virtual memory, page tables, TLBs, page faults and mmap
outcomes: Translate a virtual address with a stated page size, PTE validity and permissions.
Explain a hardware TLB miss, a recoverable page fault and an invalid access as distinct paths.
Measure first-touch versus repeated-touch fault deltas and verify private copy-on-write semantics.
Choose private versus shared mappings and identify alignment, lifetime and truncation hazards.
units.why: A valid pointer is a virtual address, not a promise of residency or a cheap access. This unit connects the CPU's translation path to kernel allocation, copy-on-write and file-backed I/O before you interpret memory totals.

next.note: Account for mappings, resident pages and retained allocator capacity.
Compare mapping and buffered reads under matched cache conditions.

study.title: Paging, translation caches and faults
study.locator: Chapter 18, Sections 18.1 to 18.4; Chapter 19, Sections 19.1 to 19.5; Chapter 20, Section 20.3; Chapter 21, Sections 21.2 to 21.5 (other chapters linked from the book contents)
study.depth: Keep the models' address widths explicit. Chapter 21's swapped-page example is not every Linux fault: demand-zero, cached-file and copy-on-write faults need no storage read. Skip replacement-policy derivations beyond the short simulator practice.

study.title: Linux fault classification and private writes
study.locator: Minor and Major Page Faults; TLB Miss, Minor Fault, and Major Fault; Measuring Page Faults on Linux; then Copy-on-Write: Initial CoW Setup, The Write-Fault Path, Frame Reference Counts and What Is Shared After fork()

study.title: Mapping semantics
study.locator: On-Demand Residency of File Pages through Mapping Lifetime and File Descriptors; Visibility vs. Durability; mmap() Versus read()

study.title: mmap API contract
study.locator: DESCRIPTION: offset, MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and MAP_ANONYMOUS; ERRORS: SIGBUS; NOTES on fork and file size
study.depth: Ignore MAP_FIXED, DAX and explicit huge-page tuning. Keep ownership of mappings separate from ownership of descriptors.

study.title: Page-table inspection and ugetpid design
study.locator: Inspect a user-process page table; Speed up system calls
study.depth: Explain the handout's entries and sketch the read-only USYSCALL lifecycle. Do not report lab execution here: QEMU and RISC-V tools are absent. Stop before Print a page table and Use superpages; implementation can follow in a provisioned xv6 checkout.

focus: Translation changes the frame number, not the offset. PTE permissions, the virtual region's policy and residency determine whether access proceeds or faults.
The x86 hardware walks page tables on a TLB miss; the kernel resolves faults. A TLB miss is not necessarily a page fault or a storage access.
Private writable pages can share frames after fork until a write fault. A sole owner may regain write permission without copying; shared mappings have different semantics.
File mappings use the page cache. Closing the descriptor does not unmap them, and MAP_PRIVATE is not a guaranteed snapshot against external file changes.
units.reproduce: Write a Python script that gets SC_PAGE_SIZE, creates a 16*1024*1024-byte anonymous mapping with explicit MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS and applies MADV_NOHUGEPAGE. Snapshot resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_minflt and ru_majflt immediately before and after writing byte value 1 at range(0, length, page_size); repeat the same pass on the same mapping. Run three fresh processes with taskset -c 2 /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I faults.py, recording CPU, kernel, Python version and all deltas. Predict first-touch minor faults on the scale length/page_size, not an exact whole-process total; the second pass already has resident writable pages unless reclaimed. Then fork, have the child set byte 0 to 2 and exit, reap it and assert the parent's byte remains 1. Close the mapping. State that this tests private semantics, not the number of physical copies or storage latency.
traps: Using Python's default anonymous mmap sharing mode and expecting private copy-on-write. Pass MAP_PRIVATE explicitly.
Counting one fault per base page without checking huge-page policy, readahead, reclamation or counter scope.
Treating successful mmap as prefaulting all bytes, or accessing a mapped file after unsafe truncation.

selfTest.q: With 4096-byte pages, VA 0x12345 and a valid VPN-to-frame mapping 18 -> 7, what is the physical byte address?
selfTest.a: VPN is 0x12 = 18, offset is 0x345 = 837, and PA is 7*4096+837 = 29509 = 0x7345, provided the access permissions allow it.

selfTest.q: How large is a linear table for a full 32-bit virtual space with 4 KiB pages and four-byte PTEs?
selfTest.a: 2^20 entries times four bytes = 4 MiB. This excludes extra metadata and is not a claim about the host's multi-level x86-64 tables.

selfTest.q: Can a resident file page cause a minor fault?
selfTest.a: Yes. The page can be in the page cache while this process still lacks a usable PTE. Installing the mapping needs no storage read.

selfTest.q: Does flushing a private file mapping publish its private writes into the file?
selfTest.a: No. MAP_PRIVATE writes belong to private copies. A shared writable mapping or explicit file writes are needed to change the backing file.

practice.name: OSTEP paging-linear-translate.py: valid and invalid translations
practice.note: Write VPN, offset, validity and physical address for every generated address before adding -c. The valid-bit model is simplified, not Linux's full fault handler.

practice.name: OSTEP paging-policy.py: a bounded resident set
practice.note: Predict hit/miss and each eviction before adding -c, then compare FIFO on the same traces. Stop at working-set pressure; do not infer Linux reclaim policy from this simulator. The section mini-project should retain the local first-touch and private-write evidence.

units.stopWhen: You solve both two-seed translation and residency exercises, classify your first/repeated-touch counters without confusing faults with TLB misses, and pass the parent/child private-write assertion.

fit.note: OSTEP supplies derivable paging models, selected AlgoMaster and mmap(2) cover Linux faults and mapping semantics, and named simulators plus the local measurement avoid an unavailable xv6 toolchain.

outcomes: Measure live requested bytes, virtual size, RSS and PSS as different quantities.
Diagnose retained allocator capacity using staged allocate/free/reuse observations.
Separate current residency, peak residency and cgroup-wide accounting.
units.why: Assume Programming's profiling-benchmarking unit; Python object-allocation profiles are background, not an RSS oracle. This unit follows native allocation into kernel mappings and distinguishes a leak from reusable retained capacity.

next.note: Diagnose memory limits using the cgroup's scope, not process RSS alone.

study.title: Library allocation versus OS mappings
study.locator: Chapter 14, Sections 14.1 to 14.3 and 14.5
study.depth: Assume ownership and invalid-free rules from Programming. Focus on why malloc/free are library calls and brk/mmap are kernel interfaces.

study.title: Allocator retention
study.locator: malloc() as a Library Function; Arenas and Chunks; What free() Does; Coalescing Adjacent Free Chunks; Obtaining Memory from the Operating System; Why free() May Not Reduce Process Memory; Multiple Arenas and Thread Caches; Observing malloc() with strace

study.title: VSZ, RSS, PSS, and What They Mean
study.locator: VSZ: Virtual Size through Comparing the Four Metrics; Reading Memory Metrics on Linux; A Hands-On Allocation Experiment; Why free() May Not Reduce RSS; Measurement Pitfalls

study.title: Mapping-level memory accounting
study.locator: DESCRIPTION: Size, Rss, Pss, private/shared fields, KernelPageSize, MMUPageSize and AnonHugePages

focus: Track requested live payload independently of allocator metadata, rounding and free chunks. The kernel accounts mappings and pages, not each application allocation.
RSS counts shared pages fully in each process; PSS apportions them. Neither is identical to the hot working set or a cgroup's charged memory.
Free returns an object to the allocator. Reuse can consume retained chunks without reducing RSS first; live neighbors can prevent returning a whole arena region.
Use smaps_rollup for detailed current totals and VmSize for mapped virtual size. ru_maxrss and VmHWM are peaks and cannot show a current-memory decrease.
units.reproduce: Build a C allocation probe with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra. At baseline and after each stage, read /proc/self/status VmSize and /proc/self/smaps_rollup Rss, Pss and private fields. Allocate 8192 blocks of 8192 bytes, checking every malloc; write through a volatile unsigned-char pointer once per sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) and at the last byte. Free even-index blocks while keeping odd ones live, reallocate those same-size blocks and touch them, then free all blocks. Print live requested payload at each stage: 0, 64 MiB, 32 MiB, 64 MiB, 0. Run three fresh processes pinned with taskset -c 2 and record CPU, kernel, GCC and glibc versions, raw snapshots and which pages were touched. Explain the observed retention or release; do not require RSS to equal payload or return exactly to baseline. A diagnostic strace -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap run can locate kernel mapping changes but is not a timing run.
traps: Calling retained free chunks a leak from one RSS snapshot. Show live ownership and bounded reuse before diagnosing growth.
Reading an uninitialized or freed block to force residency. Write while it is live and never dereference it after free.
Adding worker RSS values as physical usage, or interpreting a peak as current memory.

selfTest.q: Does malloc success prove every page has physical backing already?
selfTest.a: No. Address-space reservation and allocator bookkeeping can succeed before first-touch backing is supplied. Overcommit and later resource pressure can still cause failure.

selfTest.q: In a toy model, two processes each map 8 MiB private and the same 4 MiB shared resident pages. What are RSS and PSS per process?
selfTest.a: RSS is 12 MiB each; PSS is 8+4/2 = 10 MiB each. Their represented physical footprint is 20 MiB, not the 24 MiB RSS sum.

selfTest.q: Why might freeing alternate chunks leave residency high?
selfTest.a: Live chunks can pin the surrounding arena pages or prevent region release, and the allocator can retain free chunks. The exact behavior depends on allocator policy and layout.

selfTest.q: Can a stable peak RSS prove stable current memory after freeing?
selfTest.a: No. Peaks do not fall. Compare current snapshots and ownership over repeated workload cycles.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: staged live-byte and smaps accounting, repeated allocate/free/reuse cycles, one sparse mapping, and a diagnosis distinguishing retained capacity, shared pages and unbounded ownership growth.

Implement same-filesystem atomic replacement with checked file and directory synchronization.
Distinguish accepted bytes, visible bytes, ordered writes and durability under a stated storage contract.
Detect metadata inconsistency and payload corruption without mistaking detection for recovery.

study.locator: Chapter 39, Sections 39.1, 39.7 to 39.9 and 39.16; Chapter 40, Sections 40.3 to 40.4 and 40.6 to 40.7; Chapter 42, Sections 42.1 to 42.3 (other chapters linked from the book contents)

study.depth: Use checksum placement, misdirected/lost writes and scrubbing to separate corruption detection from redundancy-based repair.

study.title: Durability and fsync
study.locator: Accepted, Visible, Ordered, and Durable; File Durability vs. Name Durability; Durable Atomic File Replacement
study.depth: Pair with Crash Consistency: Process Crash vs. Machine Crash, Metadata Consistency vs. Application Consistency and Checksums and Validation. Keep device flush contracts and synchronization errors explicit.

study.title: File and directory synchronization contracts
study.locator: DESCRIPTION: fsync, fdatasync and directory entries; ERRORS; rename(2), DESCRIPTION: replacement, open descriptors and cross-filesystem failure
study.depth: Use https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html for the second contract. Atomic name replacement is not a power-loss guarantee.

focus: A directory maps names to inodes. Unlink removes a name; an open reference can keep the inode and data alive. Rename does not retarget existing open descriptors.

Directory search permission governs path traversal; directory write/search permission governs name changes, subject to sticky-bit and other policy. File write permission alone does not authorize replacement of its name.
A language flush sends buffered bytes toward the kernel. Successful write can leave dirty page-cache pages; background writeback is not an application commit record.

Set the new file's intended permissions before publication. Flush the language buffer, fsync the file, rename within the destination directory and fsync that directory before acknowledging durable publication under the filesystem/device contract.

Journaling can preserve filesystem metadata consistency without preserving an application's multi-record invariant. A checksum detects some damage but supplies neither atomicity nor a missing good copy.
units.reproduce:
In a private temporary directory, create state containing b'old
' and keep a reader open. Use tempfile.mkstemp in that same directory; fchmod its descriptor to 0600, wrap it with os.fdopen(..., 'wb'), write b'new
'*1024, flush and os.fsync before closing it. Call os.replace(temp, state), open the directory with O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY and fsync that descriptor before closing it. Reopen state and compare its SHA-256 with the intended payload; assert the retained reader still reads b'old
' and the published mode is 0600. Run taskset -c 2 strace -o publish.trace -e trace=openat,write,fsync,rename,renameat,renameat2,close,fchmod -- /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I publish.py. Identify the payload write, file fsync, successful rename and directory fsync in order. Check each exception and clean only your temporary files. Record filesystem/mount, kernel, Python and strace versions. This probe verifies visibility and syscall ordering, not recovered state after power loss; no power-cut test is available here.
traps: Calling close or Python flush a durability barrier, or ignoring a late fsync error and still reporting success.
Creating the temporary file on another filesystem, where rename can fail with EXDEV, or forgetting directory synchronization after publication.
Claiming a process kill simulates loss of the kernel page cache, or claiming a successful trace proves the drive honors its flush contract.

selfTest.q: After replacement, why can an old reader still see the old payload?
selfTest.a: Its open file description still references the old inode. New path lookup finds the replacement inode; rename changes the namespace, not existing open references.

selfTest.q: Why synchronize the parent directory after fsync of the new file?
selfTest.a: The file barrier covers its data and required metadata, not necessarily persistence of the directory entry naming it. The directory barrier covers publication under the supported filesystem contract.

selfTest.q: Does a metadata journal guarantee an application never reads a torn record?
selfTest.a: No. Filesystem consistency and application consistency differ. Use a record/publication protocol with validation and a stated recovery policy.

selfTest.q: Can an additive byte checksum distinguish [1,2] from [2,1]?
selfTest.a: No. Both sum to 3 modulo 256. A checksum has collision limits, and even a stronger digest cannot reconstruct lost bytes.

study.title: RAID Fundamentals
study.locator: Comparing the Common Levels; Data-Integrity Limits of RAID; RAID vs. Backups
study.depth: Optional device repair reading only. Distinguish capacity and disk-failure tolerance from corruption, deletion and independent backup recovery.

focus: Buffered read copies cache bytes into user buffers. Mmap installs mappings and faults as needed; reading one byte per block does less user-level copying than reading every block into a buffer.
Prewarm the whole file before each variant. Warm page-cache state is not a promise of warm CPU caches or installed mmap PTEs, and fsync does not evict cached pages.
HDD access combines positioning and transfer. SSD random access avoids mechanical seeks but still depends on queues, flash layout, controller policy and garbage collection.
RAID is not a backup. Corruption, application deletion and correlated failures can affect every replica or parity set; usable capacity and tolerated disk losses depend on the level.
Never drop global caches for a shared-host experiment. Reopening a file does not make it cold; a genuine device measurement needs a separately approved cache-control design.
units.reproduce: Create a private 16 MiB file of 4096 blocks, each 4096 bytes; fill block i with byte i%256, flush and fsync outside timing. Prepare orders range(4096), a copy shuffled by random.Random(7), and [(j*17)%4096 for j in range(4096)]; assert each visits every block once. Before every trial, read the full file in 1 MiB chunks to prewarm the page cache. Time with perf_counter_ns: os.pread(fd,4096,i*4096)[0] over each order; a fresh read-only mmap over each order reading mapping[i*4096]; and buffered f.read(4096)[0] in sequential order after seek(0). Include mapping creation/close in its timed scope. Sum sampled bytes; every result must equal 522240. Run five trials of every variant with taskset -c 2 /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I io.py. Record all raw times, filesystem/mount, CPU, kernel and Python versions, block size, order, prewarm and scope. Pread/buffered return 16 MiB per pass, while mmap explicitly samples only 4096 bytes and incurs page-level access. Do not call their timing ratio a device-bandwidth speedup or require a winning order.
traps: Labeling the mmap sampled-byte loop a full 16 MiB copy, or dividing every variant by file size and calling the result physical-device bandwidth.
Comparing one cold first variant with warm later variants, or keeping a mapping warm for one case while charging setup to another.
Applying an HDD scheduling model or optional RAID capacity equation as a measured property of the host's SSD.

selfTest.q: Why does stride 17 visit all 4096 block indices?
selfTest.a: 17 and 4096 are coprime. Multiplication by 17 modulo 4096 is a permutation, so the pass covers each block exactly once.

selfTest.q: What is the sampled checksum for the file?
selfTest.a: There are 16 repeats of bytes 0 through 255: 16*(255*256/2) = 522240. The file length is 4096*4096 = 16777216 bytes = 16 MiB.

selfTest.q: Does a faster warm-cache random pass show that random SSD reads beat sequential reads?
selfTest.a: No. It measures this application's warm-cache path, including syscall/copy or mapping costs. No device read or throughput claim follows without device-level evidence and cache controls.

selfTest.q: For four equal D-byte disks, what are ideal usable RAID 0, 5 and 6 capacities?
selfTest.a: 4D, 3D and 2D respectively, ignoring metadata. They tolerate zero, one and two disk failures in the ideal level model; none protects against all corruption or deletion.
